utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Good morning, ladies and gentlemen. We are back this morning, and, as I stated before we rose last night, Mrs Residovic will now have cross-examination of the witness, but, before then, could we have the appearances, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Good morning, your Honour. I am Eric Ostberg. With me today is, as yesterday, Mr Giuliano Turone and Mrs Teresa McHenry and our assistant and case manager, Mrs Ellis van Dusschoten.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Can we have the appearances for the defence in the order of the accused persons? MS RESIDOVIC (in interpretation): Good morning, your Honours. I am Edina Residovic, defence counsel of Mr Zejnil Delalic. With me is Mr Eugene O'Sullivan, Professor, and Mr Ekrem Galijatovic, attorney at law.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Can we have counsel for the second accused person? MR TAPUSKOVIC (in interpretation): Good morning, your Honours. I am Branislav Tapuskovic, attorney, defence counsel of Mr Pavo Mucic, and with me is my associate, attorney Mira Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Counsel for the third accused, please? MR KARABDIC (in interpretation): Good morning, your Honours. My name is Salih Karabdic and with me is co-defence counsel, Thomas Moran.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: And can we have counsel for the fourth accused? MR BRACKOVIC (in interpretation): Good morning, your Honours. I am Mustafa Brackovic, attorney from Sarajevo. With me in the team defending Mr Landzo is Miss Cynthia McMurrey, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Let me explain again. In all cross-examinations, or even in examinations, this order should be adhered to. If counsel decide to choose one of their number to cross-examine for the rest, that should be taken as cross-examination for the rest of them who have surrendered their chance and choose that counsel. Otherwise it would mean counsel biting twice in respect of the same cherry. So we have Mrs Residovic now, and I think this is the only time I will make that concession. MS RESIDOVIC (in interpretation): Your Honour, before taking the floor in the cross-examination, may I just say a few words linked to this decision, this ruling of yours? I think that we will thereby facilitate our task and that of the Trial Chamber. On 22nd July and 20th August, during status conferences on motions of Delalic's defence counsel for separate trials, Judge McDonald and Mr Bora drew our attention to the interest of our client in following a joint trial, because one of the decisive issues is the existence of acts for which superiors would be liable. For this reason, the defence proposed, at our previous session, that the beginning of cross-examination would start by defence counsel of those accused who are most directly linked to the act, which is a pre-condition for any possible responsibility of a superior. Therefore, I beg you, your Honour, to permit us to engage in cross-examination, whereas we would inform you every day of the order in which the counsel would cross-examine. If you could grant this, we would appreciate it very much, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Actually, the procedure I have just outlined is very simple. If you have nothing to cross-examine, you do not. Only counsel who has something to cross-examine about is the one to take the floor, and you merely say "I have no cross-examination", and that should be sufficient. MS RESIDOVIC (in interpretation): Yes, but can that be done in a different order from the one that you have indicated, that is that the counsel of those accused who are charged with the principal offence could be the first? That would be our request, if possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Please try and abide by what I have just said. MS RESIDOVIC (in interpretation): Thank you, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I add a little bit to this, in that we had asked before that the court give us guidance in this, and the court left it to the defence counsel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Actually, what I have asked is for Mrs Residovic to start her cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Let the witness return. MR ANTONIUS GERARDUS FRANCISCUS BEELEN (continued)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: You still should remind him he is under oath.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We would remind you you are still under oath?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I know. MS RESIDOVIC (in interpretation): Your Honour, may I inform you that our system is not functioning? (Short technical interruption) Mr Beelen, my name is Edina Residovic, defence counsel of Mr Zejnil Delalic. Allow me to ask you a few questions. The Celebici facility that you visited during your expert investigation, did it exist before the beginning of the war?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They told me it was before the war and it was an oil camp, and it existed before the war.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: So it was a military facility, a military barracks?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it was a military camp.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: When you visited it, was it the barracks of the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When we were there, there were soldiers in it and there were Bosnians.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Therefore it was not a camp at the time you visited it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was not a camp -- before the war it was not a camp to keep prisoners in. That was what he told me, but it was just a military camp for the storage of fuel products.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: And it was not a detention camp at the time you visited it either?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, it was not.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You used the term "camp" and "concentration camp" in your report and the sketches, because somebody told you that, in the meantime, it had been used as a camp. Those were not your words. Those were not words that you used on the basis of what you saw personally?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In Holland, we call them military base camp, military camp, so I think it is a little bit -- just a name. It had nothing to do with what kind of prisoner camp. It is just a camp for us.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You carried out measurements, and you established that the surface of the facility is about 50,000 square metres. It could be even 55,000 square metres. Is that so?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is about 50,000 square metres.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did you see the books and the layout of the facility in the books, in the land books?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the land books, no, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did you see the design documents for the Celebici facility?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, we did not.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: If in those documents you find different measurements and dimensions, would you accept that they could differ from what you said?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is possible. We just make for ourselves four measure points, and from thereon we did all our measurements, so it could be that the total area of the military base is a little bit longer or a little bit smaller than this.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You showed on video tape the path you followed in making the film. You showed us the path you took when taking the video. Did you indicate that path in your sketch?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, we did.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Which sketch, please? Is it sketch number 1?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sketch number 1.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In the table that path is not indicated. Can you show me on the sketch the path you moved along?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There is a little footpath alongside the railroad at the outside of the camp. So it ends with the little gate down there, and then it is going on to the village.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Within the facility itself, there is an asphalt road, as shown on the video. Will you show me on your sketch the facility where that road is, and what number it bears, what indication?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The asphalt road is from point 2 to point 3, and then it goes back from 4 to point 1.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Has it been included in the sketch with precision like the railway line?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it is. We took measurements of all the bends in the road and marked them on our sketch.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In taking the video, you were going along the path in front of the hangar; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Say it again?

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Were you moving along a path in front of building number 6, the hangar, when taking the video?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, we were walking on the asphalt road.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Is that the only direction that one has to follow to reach that spot?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is the usual way you go there, but you also can go over the hills and across the railroad, but that is not what we did.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Will you please show me on the sketch how you moved when you were taking the video?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We travelled the total area clockwise. So we started at the reception, the main gate. Then we walked through B to building D, and so on, until the end of the camp, to building L, it is, and then back at the side to the gate again. While we were walking, we went all around all the buildings, made photographs, made videos, and then walked along to the next building.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Could you have reached building L going from the entrance gate following the upper path?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it is possible.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: That the shorter route, is it a quicker way to reach building L?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not think so. It is about the same distance, only it is a little bit higher up.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: If you used that path to reach building L, you must have passed in front of building 6?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You mean building 6 at this side, which we called building -- what is it --

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: The building that the prosecution drew your attention to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, that is not the one that the prosecution told us. You just saw it from above, so you could see the roof of it. It is building E.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Can you see tunnel number 9 from building number 22, that you call a dispensary?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When you were in the outside, in the direction of the rail which we mentioned on our schedule, then you could see the tunnel. When you are in the other side in the direction of building D, it was not possible.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: If you were inside building 22, can you see the tunnel?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot tell you.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Can you see it from the reception, the tunnel, can you see the tunnel from the reception?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When in the room of the technician, at the far side to the tunnel, then you can see it.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Are you quite sure of that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think so, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did you check this with a photograph, by measurement, or by personal experience?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: By personal experience. We did not check it by photograph.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: I have two more questions only. You said that "A representative of the prosecution, Madam McHenry, was with us on the Thursday", when she gave you certain instructions. Was Mrs McHenry with you the second day?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, there was nobody. We just were the two of us, Mr Post and --

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did anyone give you opposite instructions to those you received from the prosecutor on the second day?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, we were brought there by an interpreter, and he said what we wanted to do, and then he left the camp, and we were just on our own.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did you personally change anything of significance following instructions from the prosecution?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, we did not.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: If the surface of the design -- according to the design documents is 84,000 square metres, and the building that the prosecution draw your attention to constitutes only 3 to 4 per cent of the total area of the facility?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We did not take measurements upside the hills and this side.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: My question is, if the design documentation gives us a surface of 84,500 square metres, is it true to say that the buildings, including the administration building, the reception and the other buildings to which the prosecution drew your attention to, constitute only 3 to 4 per cent of the total surface of the facility?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, no, all the facilities we saw are on this model.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: But what share of the total area do they represent?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The measurements we took on the base, when we were there, are marked on the plan of the camp, and those are the measurements we took and from which we put out all our measurements for the buildings.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In answer to yesterday's question of my learned colleague, you said that, if the surface was 55,000 square metres, it is about 6 per cent. If, according to the design documents, it is 84,500, is it right to say that the percentage of the surface of those buildings is 3 to 4 per cent?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I accept it.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I have no further questions. Thank you, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: I think this concludes the cross-examination of this witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Your Honour, we have recross.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: The prosecution, have you tendered the exhibits?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would now like to tender the evidences, and I think I will do it in the presence of the witness, if your Honours have any questions. As your Honours have seen through the photos, the video tape, the sketches, you can yourself judge whether this is an acceptable model of the place or not. I have been listening to the questioning. I find it hard to see why it would be improper for the witness to follow instructions of the prosecution. We have ordered this model made, and of course we have highlighted the most interesting buildings which have been made models of, and all the key things are on the model. So I now want also to say this model has a twofold purpose, of course: to visualise to your Honours what the compound looked like, but chiefly to serve as a time saving tool when we are bringing our witnesses, and make it easier for them to point out where they have been detained during their stay in Celebici. So now I would like to enter the photo book as Exhibit number 1, with the translation introductory notes as 1A, and the translation measurement -- the translation of the measurements as 2B, and I would like to enter the model as Exhibit number 2, and, by the way, I want to enter the blown-up houses. I have asked the witness, he cannot authenticate them, but I can just tell these are annexes ordered by the prosecution office to make it easier even to look into this building. They are an enlarged model of the ground plan, just as a blown-up photo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Mr Ostberg, who is tendering those ones?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: I would like to tender them just as an extra to the model.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: You are the prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: If it is objected to, I withdraw this suggestion immediately. Then we can come back to the question and enter it by the person who fabricated it. I withdraw the question of entering the bigger models. As Exhibit number 3 I want to enter the video on Celebici, which we saw during the examination of the witness. Thank you, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Your Honour, are we responding in a certain order? At this point, we would like --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: I have made it very clear that whichever way you do it, I hear counsel for the first accused, if she has anything to say. MR BRACKOVIC (in interpretation): I am sorry, there is no translation. I cannot hear the interpretation. MR TAPUSKOVIC (in interpretation): May I address your Honours?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: No. May I hear Mrs Residovic first on the position of the prosecutor in tendering the exhibits? If you have nothing to say, you pass on to the second counsel. MS RESIDOVIC (in interpretation): I have no comment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: The second, Mr Tapuskovic, if you have anything to say? MR TAPUSKOVIC (in interpretation): Thank you, your Honour, for allowing me to address you while the witness is still here. If I have understood well, I may also cross-examine the witness in the order indicated by you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: No, I do not think you have that right. You have already cross-examined him. You did that yesterday. MR TAPUSKOVIC (in interpretation): Really we find ourselves in a totally vague situation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: You cross-examined him yesterday, did you? MR TAPUSKOVIC (in interpretation): Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: You have done so. MR TAPUSKOVIC (in interpretation): I have just one question, one question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: No, there is a limit to what rights you can exercise. You cannot go indefinitely. You have cross-examined him. MR TAPUSKOVIC (in interpretation): A limit in my defence?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: He has been re-examined, and you do not have to cross-examine again. MR TAPUSKOVIC (in interpretation): But, your Honour, the defence counsel of other defendants completed their cross-examination yesterday too, and we all left so that we would have the opportunity to ask some more questions today. I have only one question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Please, Mr Tapuskovic, you have cross-examined yesterday, you have exercised your right to cross-examine, and I think that is all. If he was your own witness, you would have re-examined. That is the only circumstance in which you can ask questions again. But he is not your witness, so you cannot re-examine. MR TAPUSKOVIC (in interpretation): Thank you. It is not a very important question. I had intended to be helpful, but I will respect your ruling.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: May it please the court, your Honour, we object to defence Exhibits 1 and 2 in that they do not fully, fairly and accurately depict what they purport to depict; that is, the camp. Specifically the plan of the camp which is, I believe, included in page 3 of Prosecution Exhibit 1 differs in at least one substantial area between the model itself and Officer Beelen testified yesterday that there were several -- at least a couple of areas on the model which did not reflect what was on the ground. Therefore, your Honour, Prosecution Exhibit 2 does not fully, fairly and accurately depict the camp, and either Prosecution Exhibit 1 or Prosecution Exhibit 2 shows a proper layout. They cannot both do it, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Yes, number 4?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Yes, your Honours, if I may respond, we of course agree with Mr Ostberg to any model that will assist this court and the witnesses in the expediencies in these procedures, but what has happened here is that this model is not accurate, and only portrays the prosecution's point of view. If we can refer to the certain elevations that are very important to the defence's case that Mr Beelen and I have, and we have discussed that there are differences in here, and between now and Monday, if we can reflect it accurately so that we will be able to use it with our witnesses also, to show the inaccuracies in some of the witness statements, then of course we would have no objection to it. There are just a very few number of changes on the model that would need to be made to reflect it accurately, and, if we could work together and come to some agreement to adjust the certain elevations in this model between now and Monday, I believe that we would all be in agreement with the use of the model. It is as much an asset to our defence as it is to the prosecution's case, and so, if we can work together on that, then, by Monday -- we would certainly be able to work together and come to a common ground on this model, because it certainly is useful for both sides. We have no objection to the video tape being admitted into evidence. As far as the photographs, we have only objections to the omission of the other photographs of the camp that should have been included if this to be an impartial investigation, and we will have no objections to the model if we can make the appropriate changes on it to reflect it accurately. Also, I would like to address to the court on the issue of cross-examination, if I might just make one statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Frankly, I do not like counsel behaving most irregularly. Counsel should behave in a more courteous manner. If you get up to make comments on a particular issue, keep your comments to that issue until any other situation arises when you can add other things, and I do not like interrupting unduly. So you have made your comments on tendering of the exhibits, and I think that is all I listened to you for.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: My additional comment --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Please, I think that is all the comments you are making about the tendering of the exhibits, and that was what the Trial Chamber called you upon to do.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: We object to the admissibility of, of course, the blown-up models, because there has been no authentication whatsoever on those.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: That has been withdrawn.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: We object to the model itself unless we can make the appropriate modifications, and we agree with the video tape and the photographs, your Honour, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. We have heard the objections, and admissions of counsel. The prosecution is not pretending that someone else actually produced the model. It is their own model, and they are tendering it in evidence as their own model. If you have any other reasons during the evidence to contradict it, you are free to do so, but definitely it is admissible in evidence, and I have so admitted it. I think this is the conclusion of the evidence of this witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Yes, I am ready to dismiss the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: You can now stand down.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour. (The witness withdrew)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Any other witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour. I will now change places with Mr Giuliano Turone.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Your Honour, the prosecution calls now Mr Mirko Babic as a witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: I think it will be proper to remove those buildings, since they are no longer a part of the exercise. MIRKO BABIC (sworn) Examination-in-chief by MR TURONE

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: May I proceed?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Yes, you may.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Thank you. Sir, I am sorry, there is the ELMO exactly in between me and the witness. Sir, would you please state your full name?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I can. My name is Mirko Babic.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: And what is your date of birth, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: 21st May 1933.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Can you say what is your ethnic group?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Serbian.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: And where were you born?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the village of Bijelovcina, near Konjic, some 15 kilometres away from Konjic.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr Babic, what education did you receive? I mean, which kind of schools did you attend?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: A forester.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You mean you attended a particular school for forest guard?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: And how many years was that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Two years.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You mean two years after elementary school?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr Babic, where did you live at the beginning of May 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the village of Bijelovcina, which is my village.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: So, in May 1992 you lived in Bijelovcina, and worked there as a forest guard?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr Babic, was Bijelovcina a village with Serbian majority?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: And you said this belongs to the municipality of Konjic and the distance is about 15 kilometres from Konjic?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I object to the leading nature of the questions. He is on direct examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: I am sorry, your Honour, the witness already said that. I was just summarising what he just said a while ago.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Try and leave him to make his summaries. Leave the witness to make his summaries.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Okay. Can you say approximately how many Serbian houses, how many families, how many inhabitants did live in Bijelovcina at that time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In my village, Bijelovcina, where I lived, there were 48 Serbian homes, 5 Croatian and 4 Muslim homes.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Was there a time when Bijelovcina was affected by the armed conflict in 1992, I mean by concrete military operations in 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On 21st May 1992, around 2100 hours, my village of Bijelovcina was attacked by the Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr Babic, I will ask you in a very short while to tell us in detail what happened that day, and the following days, of course, but, before that, could you please say to the court whether you were arrested in that occasion, and detained in a military camp for a fairly long time, or not?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I am going to object again to the leading question. He is putting the words in the witness' mouth.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Should I change my question, your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Yes, ask your question more properly.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Mr Babic, would you say whether you were arrested on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I was, and I say to tell the story.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Can you please, then, tell your story from the moment at which the armed conflict started in Bijelovcina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: So, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On 21st May 1992, around 2100 hours, Muslims attacked my village of Bijelovcina. There was shooting from all directions, and myself and Boro Ivkovic, my neighbour, were sitting in front of my house. We saw that something was wrong. I went to my bedroom. I took my revolver, for which I had proper papers, and, since I was a forest guard, I had an officially issued weapon. Then I took the revolver and we started running for the woods, and then, when we reached it, I put it under a rock, and then in the woods, about 40 metres in, we stopped. There was still shooting going on all over the place. Then we stayed in that wood, and never moved from there. Within half an hour, we heard that there was some noise, there was slamming of doors and there were windows breaking, down in the house, and then --

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please, Mr Babic, slow down a little in your account, please, for interpretation to be done?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: And in Boro's house after that the noise stopped, it just stopped. So we waited in that wood, and there was gun fire all around for a while, and we spent the night there. But we talked about what to do next. We did not know what was going on. We could see the house of Boro and my house was across the ridge, and we could not see it. So we spent the night there on 22nd May 1992. The dawn came, and we went to see, over the ridge, towards my house, and, when we got there, we saw some people in green uniforms with weapons, and they were leading a few people, and then we started running, and then we went to Boro's house and stopped about 50 metres away from --

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Mr Babic, please slow down in your account.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: We object to the narrative form of the question. It should be in question answer form.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Not necessarily, please. Let him give an account of what happened to him. Yes, you can carry on.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Yes, you can go ahead, Mr Babic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Again, there was gun fire, but not in the same intervals as on 21st May. We stopped in that wood, and those who were leading the people arrived and they saw us, and then they commanded us to raise our hands, and then they told us to take off our coats and I had a hat on my head, and then I threw away the coat and the hat. Bora did not have a hat, but he had a coat, and he took off the coat and put it down, and again they told us to raise our hands, and then they said -- they cursed us and -- they started --

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Please, Mr Babic, slow down in your account.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: All right. So the first blow was in my mouth, and then they started to beat us on the chest, back. We received a lot of blows. Then they told us to follow them up the hill, which was called Lovno. Then we came up to the top of that hill, and then they wanted to see if there was something there. There was nothing there. Then there was a road down to the left side leading towards my house, and we went down the hill to the road. I saw, again, young men in green camouflage uniforms. There was a lot of them. We went and I was going ahead, and Boro Ivkovic was behind me. I remember there was a Mirsad Pirkic, and I also remember some Sejo Didik. They were walking behind us, and there were some others walking behind. About several hundred metres towards my house, about halfway, Captain Mirsad told me to stop, and I stopped. He took out some kind of a notebook from his pocket, and he said, "Come over here", so I went over to him. He tells me "Here is your brother. There is the picture". And I tell Mirsad, "No, it is not my brother". Yes. "Do you know who it is?" "That is Duro Kuljanin", and Duro Kuljanin was the President of the municipality, and so there was his membership card. I do not know where they found it, I do not know where.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr Babic, may I interrupt you for a moment, just to have you answer to some explaining question? You said you were found by soldiers in the wood. Can you say how many were these soldiers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot say anything, no.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Approximately, of course?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: But I can say there were a number of them, but I cannot say. I do not know.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Which kind of uniforms did they wear?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Green camouflage.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember if any of them had some insignia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I saw that there was a TO on the arm. That was what was written there. I could not notice anything else. On the left arm.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know who was, or who were, the commander or commanders of these men?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On the way I found out that Mirsad Pirkic was called captain, so he was the main one who was leading the other men.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: And can you say approximately at what time did this soldier find you and stop you in the woods? Was that night still, or already daylight?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On 22nd May, around 7.00 in the morning.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: All right, Mr Babic, can you go ahead in your account after this time onward, what happened to you then?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Then, when they showed me that book, belonging to Kuljanin, Mr Pirkic ordered me to eat that booklet, and I started eating it, and I ate one piece of it. I wanted to throw up, but I saw Sejo Didik from the Konjic municipality, and he kicked me in the back and so then I hid the rest of the book and then they did not see it, or something, and then we went to my house. We came to my house. The first room is where my brother is, and then on the right-hand side is my bedroom, and this is where I would take rest. I was not married. I was a bachelor. When I looked in my brother's room, I saw there were some women there, and I recognised them and I saw Novo Ivkovic and Slobodan Babic, my neighbours, and also my relative. They were bloody. Then they took me to my room, and I came there. I saw on the table there was -- they were brewing some coffee. There were about five or six people there, and they were all in green camouflage uniforms and there were also two women there. Then, when we entered the room, Mirsad Pirkic ordered that Boro Ivkovic, my neighbour, hit me, and I had to hit him. So we started hitting each other on the head. If I did not hit him hard enough, then they would hit me, and the other way round, so that Boro and I beat each other quite a bit and they laughed. Then somebody comes at the door. I think it is a soldier of theirs, and he is bringing in a stake. Not too thick, and they hit us twice over our backs with it. They took Boro out and they left me in the room. Then they put me down on the floor, and Pirkic had a hand grenade. I remember the top was like an egg, and I do not know who else attacked me, Sejo, they were beating me on my soles of my feet. They were laughing. He said, "You are resisting", and then they stopped. I saw around my table there were a lot of them surrounding me, and all of a sudden this mug came for me to drink something. When I saw what it was, it was urine, and it was bitter and they brought this coffee pot, and they poured over me, and I --

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr Babic, please, Mr Babic, speak slowly. Could you say again who gave you this urine?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As I noticed, I saw one man in camouflage uniform, and on his hand was "U". I think it was Zeljko Mlikota from the Konjic municipality, and Mia Mladen. They gave me that urine to drink.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Okay, go ahead, please, but very slowly, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: After the urine that I drank, those two women, I do not remember them very well, I think that maybe I remember one. I think that maybe it was Alagic, I do not know if that was Safija or Nora.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Just a moment, please. We are more concerned with the charges in the Celebici camp. The evidence which is being related, does it relate to Celebici camp, happening in the Celebici camp?

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Your Honour, this is --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That will come, that will come, once I make it there.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: It is the trip on the way, I would say. So it is relevant, because of something which happened in between. So it is relevant to what --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: To what charge does it relate, all this evidence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I will go on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: To what charge does it relate, all this evidence?

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: It will be clear that it will be related at least to one of the deaths having occurred inside the camp later on, but it will be clear later on, your Honour. This is not going to be a very long account of something happening outside the camp. May I proceed? Yes, Mr Babic, you can proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: So those two women were in green camouflage uniforms. They continued to beat me over the head. One of them was holding a fork in front of my eyes, and threatened to gouge them, and then they had a bayonet, and then they were breaking glass and they were bringing sharps in front of me and they were cursing me and saying, "Look how bloody you are". Then they beat me for a while and then they stopped. Then two people were brought their boots for me to lick them, and I had to lick, and there was earth on them, and then that lasted not very long. In the end, Mirsad Pirkic, the captain, asked me where my revolver was. I told him that I left it in the woods under a rock above from Boro's house, and it was properly issued to me in 1967 by the MUP in Konjic, and I had it as a forest guard, and Pirkic went with me where I left the revolver, and the permit. When I came to that place, I showed the revolver. Mirsad took the revolver and the permit. He tore up the permit, and kept the revolver. Then we went back to my room. They were all still in the room, and Mirsad says, "All right, let us move", and everybody left, except for me and Mirsad. Then I left later with him, and Novo Ivkovic, Babic Slobo and Boro Ivkovic, who was with me, and with whom I exchanged --

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: I beg your pardon, Mr Babic, I beg your pardon, can you say did you in any way take part in the defence of the village of Bijelovcina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. I was 60 years old. I was not interested in defending. I was going to do my own job.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: So at what time did you leave your house in that day, then?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Somewhere around 11.00.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: And what happened to you after that? Were you taken to any specific place?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is what I want to say.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The people in my room, Bora, Bosa, Ivkovic Anica and Ivkovic Danica, we all came out and we saw three green boxes, and they ordered me to carry one of them, and the other one Noro -- Boro Ivkovic carried the other and Slavko took my box. I do not know if somebody told him that he did not -- that he did not have to, but he took it. Then we went to the house of Slavko Tomic in Bijelovcina, the same street, and that is where we stopped. Pirkic ordered that we should all stop and turn facing east, and to close our eyes. One woman started crying, because for her it meant execution. At that point, somebody called from the field, called him, and that was stopped. Then we came, and we stopped at the next house, and there were bringing some brandy from that house, and we sat there. After that, we moved on. Sejo Didik separated me out and said, "Now we are going towards Uras Djukic's house". He started kicking me in the house and beating me all over. I started waling and saying, "Do not", but nothing helped. Then we came to Djukic's house. There was some wood in front of that house, and he ordered me to move this wood from one place to another. Whenever I would bend down, he would kick me with his soldier's boot. He beat me really terribly. I will never forget that.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr Babic, was there any other prisoner at that time with you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At that time, no, I was the only one. All the rest of them were all at Boco Tomic's house at that time, and then he took our bayonet, and pointed at my stomach and mistreated me there, and Captain Mitke -- there were five or six of them, plus the two women, and then we moved on, and then they said, "You are going to be the guide today". So I took them to the -- to the village of Vinjiste by the way that was easier, but they did not want that. They wanted the other way. They were on the -- on the right-hand side there were rocks, and then they were going down. I said, "Do not go down there, because there are rocks there", and then they cursed me again, and then they said, "Where are you leading us, we will all die here". Then we stopped. So then there were two hills, and there was a river in between. To the right, there is a wood, and on the left-hand side, there is nothing, no vegetation there. When we came down by the rocks from near a wood, all of a sudden there was gun fire coming. Fortunately, they were not coming in our direction. Then they commanded me, Mitke did, to take the path, and twenty, thirty metres later, they ordered me to stop and lie down. And then he called the rest, and about 500 metres later we came to a clearing, and then we sat down. At that moment, I saw two women. There was something --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Mr Turone, the Trial Chamber will rise for about fifteen minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: I am sorry, Mr Babic, we are going to have an interruption for fifteen minutes, and we will start again after fifteen minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: 11.30. (11.15 am) (A short break) (11.35 am)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Let the witness come in. Kindly remind him he is still on oath.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: May I remind you that you are still under oath?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I am continuing my travel. I said that we reached the woods. We sat down, and then those two women took Slobo Babic, and they put some things on him to carry, and then we all sat down. When we sat down, they would call me, and they hit me on the head. They did the same to Slobo. A little way away, they took out a rope. I do not know what they were doing.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr Babic, excuse me interrupting you, is this Babic the same Babic you were talking about earlier, or another Babic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, the same Babic, Slobodan Babic. Are you thinking of the trip? I did not see Slobodan Babic before we reached the woods.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Please, Mr Babic, speak very slow to us. Can you say to us who is this Slobodan Babic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Slobodan Babic is my relative. We live next door, we lived as neighbours. My father and his grandfather were brothers, so that we were cousins.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: So do you mean this Slobodan Babic joined you at a certain moment after leaving your house?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Shall I continue?

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, you can continue. Can you tell us at this very moment, were there any other prisoners with you, or only you and Slobodan Babic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There was just me and Slobodan Babic.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: And who were the other people surrounding you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: With us, with us people who were chasing us, who were forcing us to go along the road, Sejo Didik, those two women, and some others. Shall I continue?

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, you can.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Then we moved on, and Sejo Didik told me, he called me a "cetnik", he called me "cetnik" the second time, I kept quiet, the second time I said, "I am not a "cetnik". Then he said if you do not answer my call, I will kill you. Then we went on. I wanted to lead them along the road, but they chose another path through the woods, and Sejo called me "cetnik" a couple of times, and I had to answer, and they laughed. We went through the woods, and we reached a river called Uguscica and there we stopped. I asked whether I could drink, take a drink of water and they would not let me. Then we had to go along the right side to reach the village of Vinjiste. I went in front, and every twenty or thirty steps, they would say "Stop". I stopped, and we went on until we reached the village of Vinjiste and the house of Nikola. Then they forced me to go inside, to knock on the door to see who was inside. I knocked and Nikola Zuza, his wife and son-in-law, Rajko Miluntinovic, Milan Savic --

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Speak slower, Mr Babic, please, speak slower to us.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: -- came out of the house. They came out of the house, and in front of Nikola's house, there was some water. There was a tap, and I asked to drink, and they let me. So I had a drink. Slobodan also had a drink of water. We were allowed to drink, and then we went on some thirty metres from Nikola's house. Then he took me aside, and Slobo Babic to another side.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Who took you aside, Mr Babic, who took you aside?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The Captain Pirkic, Mirsad Pirkic, and they were about 30 metres away from us, and they were consulting, they were pointing in various directions. I did not know what. Then Captain Pirkic came up to me and sat down, and he said, "My dear forest guard, you have been good, you were our guide, and you served us well. For me, you are a legend, but we are leaving you here". He threatened with executions, hanging or tearing me up, but, "The best solution for you is death. One of us will put a bomb in your mouth, and then this man will pull out the wire, open your mouth and that is the easiest death for you". I begged the captain, I said, "My dear captain, do not kill me", I pleaded with him. He said he could not do anything. He went back to his group. He talked to them and again sat next to me. He said to me, "When we head for that village of Homolje, you will go in front of me. I cannot protect you. I doubt you will live. They will kill you." When we moved, I was on the right, and Slobo was on the left-hand side. My legs were swollen from the beatings. I could feel that my ribs were broken, and I could hardly move. I was thinking of asking them to shoot me, but I did not. Then we walked for about one hour, and we reached the village of Homolje. It is a Muslim village. There we sat down. Me and Slobodan Babic, we lent against a wall.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr Babic, at what time approximately did you arrive at Homolje?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It may have been perhaps an hour before dusk, before nightfall.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Can you say approximately which was the distance you covered between Bijelovcina and Homolje?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think about ten -- eight to ten kilometres. I cannot tell you exactly. Shall I continue?

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: When you arrived at Homolje, you were together with Slobodan alone, or had other prisoners joined you in the meantime?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There was no one else, just Slobodan Babic and me, no one else.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In what condition was Slobodan Babic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was covered in blood, like me, and we just kept quiet. There was nothing we could do. There were five or six metres between us, and we sat there for about one hour, and then night fell. It was raining. A lorry came up and we all climbed into it. Some went into the cabin. We were sitting in the back, and Captain Mirsad Pirkic was next to us, and he was singing some songs, some silly songs. This did not last long, and so we reached the sports hall of Musala in Konjic. Me and Slobodan were put in room number 10, and in that room I found my neighbours, and we spent the night there. About midnight, Slobodan Babic was called out, and they kept him outside for a long time. Then he came back, and then they called me out. I went out into the corridor, and I saw the investigators there. One of them I could recognise, and he recognised me, Pajic Mirsad from Konjic municipality. They asked me what had happened to me. I did not dare tell them what had happened, because I was covered in blood. I just said that I had fell, and hurt myself. I was ordered to sit down in the corridor. Then they asked me some stupid questions, did I vote for SDS? I said, "Yes". They were not very dangerous, and again I went back to room 10, and Slobodan and I spent the night there. Then it dawned. That was 23rd May 1992. Then, when night fell, they called out me and Slobodan. There was a lorry. We entered it, and we went about one kilometre from Musala to a locality called Radava, it was a hotel. I do not know exactly whether it was Radava or Neretva. We climbed down from the lorry, entered this hotel, and immediately at the door they started beating us and cursing our mother. One woman, this is something I have to say, she was a great help to us. She knew me well, and she said, "You will not hit the forest guard". It seems that she was working in that hotel. She must have been a cook or something. She brought us some boiled eggs, and we asked her to bring us some water, because we were very thirsty. She brought us some water, because we had lost a lot of blood, and I am very grateful to her. We sat there for about half an hour, and then we were ordered to move again. I had lost my senses. I did not know where I was going, or what I was doing. I was simply out of my mind. We went down the steps. The lorry was waiting. I climbed up. I do not know what happened to Slobodan. Whether he climbed up or not, whether there was anyone there or not, I really do not know. The lorry started moving, and I reached Celebici on May 23rd, and I was put in building 22. When I entered, I saw lots of prisoners there. It was so densely populated that we could hardly stand. There was Spaso Vukalo, there were some other neighbours. I was badly hurt, and I saw a pump, a machine, I do not know what kind of machine --

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: May I interrupt you for a moment, Mr Babic? When you reached Celebici on a truck --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At night, on 23rd.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: At night, at about what time, do you remember approximately?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The evening.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Were there any other prisoners in that lorry, in that truck that led you to Celebici?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot remember anything. I was lost. I remember I was there, and I do not know whether there were any other people in that truck. I simply do not know. I cannot say, because I was really very sick, and I spent the night there. As far as I can remember, about two days later, I saw Pedrac Babic, the son of Slobodan Babic, in this same building 22, and I saw Slobodan Babic lying down in this building 22. He could not see anything. He could not hear. I thought he was dying. I think he was there for about eight days. His son disappeared, Spaso, Drago. But many of us were left. Slobodan was moved away, and I do not know anything, but I heard later that he died on March 3rd.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Could you describe in more detail the physical conditions of Slobodan Babic when you saw him in number 22 in Celebici?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was in a very grave condition. His lips were injured. Something was broken in his mouth. A bottle of water appeared from somewhere, and those who were next to him, they poured drop by drop of water into his mouth, but it could not go down, because his throat, everything was hurt. He was in a very bad condition, all broken up. I really do not know. (redacted) and Dr Petko Grubac will be able to tell you more, because he died there, and they were there when he died.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Can you explain to the court who are Dr Grubac and (redacted)?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You mean of nationality, what nationality they are? (redacted) is from Bradina and Dr Petko is from somewhere in Montenegro. He worked in a health centre, and I knew them very well.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You mean they can say something in detail about the conditions of Slobodan Babic for which reason?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Slobodan Babic died on 3rd March in the presence of (redacted) and Grubac.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you describe in detail this building number 22 you were in?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can hardly describe it. I just know that it was rectangular in shape. I really cannot describe it. I know there were a lot of people inside. There was not room to sit down.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Can you say approximately how many people were there inside there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I could not say. I do not know.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Can you say how were the conditions of life in building number 22?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The conditions were terrible. There was very little water, and very little food. The hygiene was very poor. I do not know.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: What about the toilet facilities?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I saw some people going out. There was a toilet outside. I saw that. Maybe for twenty days, I did not go to the toilet at all, and I am surprised. I do not know how come, from 21st May, until 23rd May, I spent some twenty days there in building 22. I never went out. I do not know how that was possible, but there you are.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr Babic, if you should see a map or a model of the camp of Celebici, could you recognise it and indicate 22 in that, or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I could not, no, nothing. I had never been in that camp before. I came there at night. I was ill, and I really could not help you with any maps.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Can you say approximately how long did Slobodan Babic remain in building number 22?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It seems to me about eight days.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: How do you know about what happened to him later?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When I left the camp, I met some people, (redacted), and he told me.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You told us that you stayed in number 22 for a number of days. How many days, do you say?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I think about twenty days.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: And after that, what happened to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Shall I continue? I was there for some twenty days. Nobody hurt me. I was moved to number 6. When I got to number 6, I saw four rows of people, one row in a circle and two rows across the middle. There were about 250 prisoners. Hazim Delic put me in the third row, six from the door, and that is -- that was my place. I do not know, I think it must have been about the 15th June. They said some journalists would be coming, and people came. They were black. Delic was there and some others talking to them. I do not know what they were talking about, and the journalists left, and after the journalists, Esad Landzo came. He took Branko Gotovac, took him out. What he did to him, who knows? When Branko Gotovac came back, he fell. He could not breathe. Fortunately, there were two nurses, medical technicians, who pulled his tongue out of his mouth, Branko, so he started breathing again. Branko was very seriously ill. They moved him to some sort of dispensary, and Branko was there. Then one day Delic Hazim came and said to his son, Danilo Branko, his son, "Do you know your father has died?", and he said, "Let him". But Branko did not die, he came back, he recovered.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Can you give us a description of this hangar number 6?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Maybe a little. I think it was again rectangular in shape. I know it had an iron roof structure, and that is all I know about it.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: What about the size of this building number 6? Do you know approximately how many people could fit there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know. It was quite wide. Maybe three times as many people could fit.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: What about again conditions of life, food, toilet facilities in this place?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were no conditions. It was very bad. We sat on the concrete floor. It was dirty. The hygiene was terrible. There was a bucket behind the door for toilet purposes. There were five spoons for 250 of us. Five would go and eat. Sometimes there was something cooked, and this meal took about two hours. Somebody would take a little more. Then the next person had nothing. There was very little bread. We were all hungry. In July, we had nothing to eat for 56 hours. I remember that.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Can you mention the names of some other prisoners who were with you in building number 6?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I can remember Vule Mrkajic, Risto Vukala, and then some of my neighbours too.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr Babic, did you personally suffer physical maltreatment during your stay at Celebici?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can tell you that I personally was not hurt, but, when I came from 22 to 6, after about three days in the evening they called me out. I do not know who it was. It was dark, and some hit me with iron spades about five or six times, and then they sent me back to my place. That was once, and I can also remember somewhere after 20th July in 1992, one morning, Hazim Delic, he came and he kicked me with his boot, and he passed by me. Another day, again about 9.00, he came and again he kicked me with his boot. A third day, again, about 10.00, he kicked me a third time, and then he left. He walked past the rows, he went out. Then about an hour later, he called my name, "Come out". I went out. I saw Esad Landzo, and a third man, whom I did not know. They took me some fifteen metres from the door. Landzo Esad put a mask over my eyes, and they started beating me.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Please speak very slowly, Mr Babic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They beat me. I was virtually unconscious. Three of them were beating me. When they took the mask off, I saw Delic, Esad Landzo and this third man. I know Hazim Delic, because he worked with me in my enterprise. He was a good man. His father was Ibro, I know him too, he was a good man too, and I know Hazim Delic, because he worked with me in the same company. I begged Hazim, "Do not do this". I begged him two or three times. He cursed my mother, and he would not let the other two to beat me. But Esad Landzo kept on beating me all the time, and then he told me "hurry up" to reach the door. There was a plank holding the gate, and, when I reached the gate, Esad Landzo opened the door, took the plank and hit me with it, and I fell in front of the door and I knew nothing more. I was in a coma. Probably no one dared touch me.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Please speak very slowly, Mr Babic. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I could feel a fever coming, and something cold on my head. Somebody must have been pouring water over my head, and I regained consciousness. I was in a very bad condition. I did not know anything from then on. To days later, Esad Landzo came up, kicked me with his foot, and told me to get up. He took me out, and to the same spot where I had been beaten, and he told me to lie down.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Excuse me, if I could interrupt you, Mr Babic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was sunny.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In which place inside the camp was that occurring?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Maybe fifteen metres from the door.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: From the door of what?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: From the door of the building.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Of which building?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: From building 6.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Can you say approximately in which time did this happen, or at least very approximately in which time did this happen?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Somewhere around 12.00.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: I mean not only the real time, but the period of time, which week, which month at least?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was after -- around 20th July 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: May I go on?

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You can go ahead, yes. Very slowly, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Esad Landzo ordered me to lie down. I did. He told me to uncover my legs, to lift my trouser legs, so I was bare. He held a bottle in his hand and he asked me, "Do you know what this is?" And he had a knife in his hand. I said, "I do not know", and he opened this bottle, and poured some stuff on my right leg, and I could smell that it was petrol, and then he set fire to my leg. I saw the flame. It was very painful. I almost lost consciousness. This did not last very long. He covered that leg up, and he told me to get up. He kicked me a couple of times. He went back to the door. I removed the plank. I went in, and sat down. What happened later with my leg, some blisters and burns and there was a yellow liquid pouring from that leg. So I did not know where the pain was worse, in my chest, my head, my legs, my burns. I could not stand up any more, and Hazim Delic knows well. He would come in the afternoon, about 3.00, and he would take fifty men in front of building 6. There was a canal there. There was water, and he would select those fifty men to urinate and then the next 50 would go there. As I could not stand up alone, Dragan Tomic would help me, and he would lead me there, and back, and it happened like this on a daily basis. That is how I lived throughout that period. I was quite incapable of doing anything. I can also remember somewhere around 1st or 8th August, the International Red Cross came to visit number 6.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr Babic, we will see that later. Before that, I would like you to describe the physical consequences which you suffered after the detention at Celebici. Can you describe the physical consequences on your body after that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can. I have three teeth knocked out and fractured ribs, and I also have consequences of the burns when Esad Landzo poured gasolene over me.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Are you in a condition, Mr Babic, to show to the court, if you wish -- is that scar fill visible on the leg?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it is visible, and I can show it.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Could you show to the court this -- the scar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: How shall I do it?

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You can maybe move around, maybe somebody could help him to have this shown to the court. I do not know whether the camera can show in a proper way this leg?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Let him speak to the microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: You can go back to your seat now.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Your Honour, could we as defence counsel just approach to see the wound?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Yes, I suppose so.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: The defence counsel wish to see the injury.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: May I proceed, your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Yes, you can.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Mr Babic, did you actually know Mr Delic from before the war?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I knew him. I knew him well.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Can you explain better how come you knew him from before the war and how long a time before?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I knew him for a long time. He worked for the same company for which I worked, but he was a different unit. That was called mechanisation unit. I do not know what he was by trade, but I think he did something with trucks there, and we knew each other well. We greeted each other and never felt anything -- we never had much contact. We never talked much. But, with his father, I was very good friends with Ibro.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Where was this common activity located?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was a transportation company. I do not know what it was called, and so that was a mechanisation or mechanical unit. It was a company that hauled timber, and I do not know what that particular unit of that company was called.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: And where was this company?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is about 100 metres from the railway station towards Ovcari.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr Babic --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am sorry, that was when the narrow track railroad was still there. That is where they kept the trains, and that is where Hazim Delic worked, in that unit, which was located there.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Can you say in which years was that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: All the way until the war, but I do not know for how many years, maybe five or six, up until the outbreak of the war he worked in that company.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr Babic, can you say which function did Delic have inside the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We called him, when he would come, Mr Commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Excuse me, your Honour, unless he can show he has personal knowledge of what Mr Delic's job was, his title, we object on lack of personal knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: I did not get the question, I am sorry. I did not get the objection.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: The objection is that, unless the witness can show personal knowledge of what Mr Delic's function in the camp was, we would object that he has no personal knowledge, and, therefore, cannot testify as to his job.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: I might ask the witness, if you wish, do you know anything about the function of Delic inside the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I believe that he was some kind of commander, because we addressed him as "Mr Commander". Now, I do not know what function it was that he had, but we called him "Mr Commander", so that is how it was. I think he was something to do with Pavo Mucic, his deputy, or something like that. I do not know that, but he was high, he had a high function. He was there all the time. He was entering every day. I saw people beating Vukalo Kajic and others, but, when he would enter, everybody was in fear. Almost -- your heart would almost burst, and I can say that, until 20th July, he never touched me, and, had I not been beaten then, I certainly would not be here today.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did you know Mr Landzo from before the war?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, very little, nothing. I knew him later very well, because he never left the camp. He had an underground shelter near number 6, and I think that he was spending nights there, and, whenever he wished, he would enter and he was committing grave crimes on different people, I can say that much.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did you ever hear about Esad Landzo before the war about his name?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can say that I know his father quite well. He worked in the same company where I worked, and he had an uncle, Nuro, and we were great friends. We went to Spajan Forest together. We were inseparable, but I am interested how was he born that way, and who told him this, and who taught him how to do these things, to do these stupid things to other people, from such a family, that kind of man.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: What relationship did you have with his father and uncle?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: With the uncle, a very good relationship, and I only knew his father as an acquaintance.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: And did you know that this man had a son by the name Esad?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I did not know that. Only after I left the camp I have neighbours who went to school with Esad Landzo, young people.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr Babic, do you know about physical maltreatment suffered by other prisoners inside Celebici camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can say something about that. Some time in the middle of July --

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Your Honour, we object to this --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Should he give evidence of other --

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: We object to his testifying to what happened to other people in the camp, unless they can prove that he has some personal knowledge about what happened to other people in the camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: May I state the question in a different way?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Actually, you may have to phrase the question in a way that he has to tell you what he knew of what he saw.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: May I say do you have any personal direct knowledge of maltreatment suffered by any other people?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do. I can say -- can I continue?

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Some time in mid-July, maybe -- June, maybe early June, Esad Landzo came to the camp, to number 6, and asked who is Bosko Samoukovic, and Bosko said, "It is me" and he had a piece of wood in -- a stick in his hands, and he told him to get up and put his hands behind his head, and then he beat him up in the back, and he fell down. Then he took him out, and then I do not know anything more, but we heard that Bosko Samoukovic died later.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I object. He does not have any personal knowledge to what he heard; what he saw is appropriate.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: But I saw.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: If he saw it, then of course, but I do not think he had personal knowledge when he said he was taken out of the hangar, and he does not know. Could we ask it be limited?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: You can say that he died, he did not come back, he died.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I heard that he died in the infirmary somewhere, I do not know where, I do not know about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: May I proceed, your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Can you go ahead, Mr Babic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The second victim was some time after June 15th. They brought Scepo Gotovac, Hazim Delic, Adem Cosic and Esad Landzo, and they put him behind the door. They got outside, and that was around 12.00. That was day time, and Scepo sat there, maybe one hour, I do not know how long, and the door opened, and Hazim Delic came to the door to take Scepo Gotovac and Adem Cosic was there and next to Hazim was Esad Landzo and Hazim Delic tells Scepo Gotovac to get up, and he did, and he told him, "Scepo Gotovac, you killed on 29th March for the two Muslims, so we will kill you here". Scepo said, "I never killed anyone", and he cursed his mother, and --

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: A little slower, Mr Babic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: And kicked him and then Scepo fell down on the concrete, and the three of them took him out, and I heard wailing, and I heard something like blows and then I started counting, then I stopped, and then they threw him back in. Scepo was still alive, and he sat on the concrete behind the door maybe an hour or two later, again Hazim Delic came to the door, and Hazim and Esad, and also told him the same thing as the first time, and Adem Cosic had a knife in his hand and they took him by hands and feet, and Hazim put a knife next to him and they took him out and then beat him again, and then he was again wailing and --

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Slower, please, Mr Babic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Then they put him back in. Then they threw him back in. He had something on his forehead. I do not know what it was. I thought it was like a badge or something. I do not know if they put something on his forehead, and Scepo Gotovac was dead. I do not know what it was, and in the morning, they took him out, and I do not know anything about Scepo any more. That is the second victim. The third victim. Late July/early August of 1992, in the morning, around 7.00, some certain Dragolub Kujundzic, called Gago, he was called out by a guard, this Kujundzic, and it took about ten minutes, and then Klimenta Zeljko, who was also called Keljo, they called him out to drink coffee and then ten minutes later there was a gun shot, and Kujundzic Gago ran inside, and said "Keljo is dead", and he cried. So that is the third victim I know, and I do not remember the fourth victim. I do not know the date very well. Cedo Avramovic, he was called out in the evening. We did not hear anything.
