He was held outside, and then he came to the door, and he went to his place. In the morning we found him dead on the floor. Then I remember the other ones. I remember Pero Mrkajic, Simo Jovanovic, and I remember some others, but I know that Esad Landzo beat Simo Jovanovic for three days, and those people disappeared.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I object. Excuse me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know where these people finished.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: We object to him testifying about these other three people, that he just said they were beaten. He has no personal knowledge. The prosecution has not qualified him as having any personal knowledge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Actually, have you been listening to what he is saying?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour, I have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: First listen to what he said, and then object. I think that is a better way, if you listen and then you find that he is not testifying to his personal knowledge of what he has seen and heard, and then object to it. Let us hear him say what he said.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Okay, you can go ahead, Mr Babic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As I spoke about the victims as I could see, and I also know people who were disappearing, whom I remember. I could not see well all the time I was sick, and others saw better than I did. As far as I remember, there were nine victims in number 6, and what I saw, I did see, and I can prove that.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr Babic, can you say who was the commander of the camp then?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. I did not know who it was. When I left the camp, I heard that the camp commander in Konjic was Zejnil Delalic, but I do not know anything else about him.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Were there any occasion in which we could meet Mr Mucic in the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I had several opportunities, but I did not know him. He would come there infrequently. He came once. There was a man, they called him "Tarzan", and he talked to him some and then he left. And then -- but I did not know him then. So I saw him twice. He would come in, and somebody would say, "This is the commander".

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: What do you mean "come in"? Come in where?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: To the camp, all the way to the door. He would step in, make two steps, and then he would talk to Tarzan, and then he left. That is when I saw him entering.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You mean the door of what?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That was number 6 in the camp, and the door opened, and he entered, and he stood at the door, and to the right, next to the door, was this older man, Tarzan, and then he talked to him, and then, after a while, he left. And that is what I saw.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: And did Mr Mucic wear a uniform?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, a green camouflage uniform.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did you know Mr Mucic from before the war?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know who was Mr Mucic's superior, if you are aware of this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: According to others, it was the camp commander in Konjic.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: I did not get the answer, Mr Babic. My question was did you know --

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I object to that question. Again, a lack of personal knowledge. It has not been established.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: I do not know what you mean by "personal knowledge". Whether he knew who was the camp commander, he was an inmate of the camp, was he not?

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: And what else?

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: He is being asked who is the superior.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Possibly, if he was familiar with the place in which he was a member, it is likely he would know. He may be wrong, but maybe that is his knowledge of the place.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: May I proceed? Have you any knowledge of who was -- I am sorry?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Yes, please go on with your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: May I proceed?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: My question --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: May I proceed about Pavo Mucic?

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: My question is have you any knowledge of who was the superior of Mr Mucic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, Hazim Delic.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Do you mean Delic was the superior of Pavo Mucic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know who was superior, who was older, I do not know that.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: When I say "superior", I do not mean "older". I mean superior in his rank.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: He has answered your question. He did not know who was the superior. I think that is conclusive.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: That is all right, okay. Were you ever interrogated by military investigators during your stay in Celebici?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: And when and where in the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In 22. I was taken out one day and they asked me what I had in terms of weapons, and I told them that I had a revolver with a permit since 1967, that it was issued by MUP in Konjic and after that they did not ask me much. They put me in 22, and then I was not called out any more.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember how many people did interrogate you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think there were three of them sitting there around -- behind the table, not more than three.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember or know their names, or the name of any one of them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I know one of them, Miro Stenek from Konjic.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Were they in uniform?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they were -- no, I cannot recall, because that was in the evening when they took me out.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: And I could not see well. I had had enough of life by that time.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr Babic, were you accused of anything specific by these three investigators?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I was not accused of anything.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did you sign any piece of paper after the interrogation on their request?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I did not sign anything.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Was that a long interrogation? How long did it last?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, that was very, very short. Maybe five or six minutes.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Was there any judicial proceedings against you after that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, there was nothing, no, no legal proceedings.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr Babic, did the Red Cross ever visit the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: How many times?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Around 1st August, it was the first time when the International Red Cross came to number 6, and they entered by themselves. There was nobody else but them. They closed the door behind them, and they questioned us for some two hours on what the situation was, whether we were beaten, whether we had anything to eat, what was the discipline, whether there were any crimes, and some responded, and then they were showing them burns. Esad Landzo had built some fire, and Vulo Mrkajic and Vukalo, and he burnt them with some iron bar.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Your Honour, we object. What he is saying right now, it has not been proven that he has any personal knowledge about any fire or burning of somebody by Esad Landzo. He is just talking from hearsay right now, or from no personal knowledge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Let us hear your question again.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: My question was -- pardon, Mr Babic, my question was, did the Red Cross ever visit the camp, and you said yes. How many times, and what happened on that occasion? This was my question, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I will continue. So the International Red Cross called us individually, us who were burnt and who were injured, to show the wounds, and some went over there, but I did not dare go. So it was about two hours that it all lasted, and then they left, and they said that they would come back in about ten days. About half an hour later, Hazim Delic comes, and some others with him, and he had something like a wooden bat. It was wider at the top, and he cursed us, and he said, "What were you talking?", and we all got beaten. So ten days later, the International Red Cross came again. It was 12th August 1992. They came the same way into --

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Speak slowly, please, Mr Babic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Number 6, and we told the International Red Cross, "Do not come here, because we are being beaten because of you". And then they said, "Do not be afraid, just raise your hands who was", and some did, and they said, "They will not beating any more", and then again for two hours they talked to us again, asked us when we were detained, took down dates, and registered us. Then, they called me again, and they asked me to show my right ankle, and then they looked at it, and registered it, took it down in writing. And on 12th August 1992, after that time, it was better. There were no beatings, nothing. Then we started receiving visits from home. There was food coming from home. It was better, so.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Can you say when did you leave Celebici camp, Mr Babic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I can. 1st September 1992, around 12.00. Pavo Mucic came to the door. He came inside, followed by Hazim Delic, and at the door, the first people, they asked them what they had in terms of weapons, and every third or fourth was sort of called out by Delic, and they were leaving, and then my turn came, and he asked me, "What kind of weapon did you have?" I said, "A revolver with a permit". "You are the forest guard?" "Yes". He said, "Step out". And the Red Cross was there about fifteen metres away, and I crossed over to them. They marked something. There was a van, and I entered. There was a lot of us, and we went to Musala Sports Centre in Konjic. Then I was again put in room number 10, and there --

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Okay, Mr Babic, just a moment, please. When you left Celebici camp, you said on September 1st, was Mr Esad Landzo still there as a guard?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Five or six days, he did not come to the camp. Whether he came back, I do not know.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: So when you left the camp, Mr Landzo was not there any more?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, he was not.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: And when had he left before that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know. Maybe five or six days before I left. I left on 1st September. He simply disappeared. I never saw him again. But before that, he would enter daily.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr Babic, just shortly, how long were you kept in Musala after leaving Celebici?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I got there on 1st September 1992, and I left the sports hall at Konjic on 24th September for the camp of Trnovo near Kalovnik. I spent only 24 days in Konjic, the camp.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You mean in Trnovo and Musala, yes. What about Trnovo? How long did you stay in Trnovo?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I went to Trnovo, and I stayed from 24th September until 12th October 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: And what happened then?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was in Trnovo. It was the same kind of treatment as in number 6, only they did not beat us. They would come during the day, three of them, with arms in camouflage uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, but how long, the time you remained in there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I stayed there from 24th September 1992 till 12th October 1992, so you know how many days.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: And what happened after that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: What happened was that one day, this was on 12th in the afternoon, they came, three men, armed men came to the door, and they pointed at me and told me to come out. I went out. There was Radan Bendo, who was also taken out. There were some white rags, and they tied my eyes. They blindfolded me, and I had to climb up into the truck, and this Bendo, his eyes were blindfolded too. And then for three kilometres, this truck went on. Then somebody led me by the arm, and I later learnt it was Rogo, and they asked me whether I could see, and I said I could not. We went down the slope, and then they started swearing at us, our Serb ethnic mothers, and then I fell on something hard.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did you still remain prisoner after October 12th?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Let me just tell you, no, I was not. They took me out. I fell on something hard, they took off the blindfold. I saw a road, and a forest, and this man I learnt later his name was Zuric, he was deputy police chief in Trnovo. He told me, "You have five kilometres to go from here. There is no one there. It is a buffer zone. Be careful. It is all mined. Go and join your people. If you get killed, you get killed". When he took off the blindfold, I saw Bendo Radan too, and we went together straight ahead, and we walked about five kilometres, and the place is called Dobropolje. There were three people also wearing camouflage uniform in our direction. I did not know what to do, because I know that people in camouflage uniform had beaten us before, and then, as we got closer, they said, "We are Serbs". It was the Serb Army, and about 200 metres from the barracks, we sat -- they took us inside, a car came to pick us up, and from Dobropolje, it is 20 kilometres by road, and they took us to Kalovnik. When we got to Kalovnik in the police station, the MUP, I had 39 kilos. They weighed me. I weighed 39 kilos. And that was my story from May 22nd 1992 until 12th October 1992. I have nothing more to say. Five years have gone by since. I cannot remember everything. One forgets. Only the scars remain and the wounds one cannot forget.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: All right, Mr Babic, thank you very much. Your Honour, I have finished my examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you too. May I go?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: No, not for the time being.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Just wait for a moment, please, Mr Babic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: We would have wished to continue, but I think it is almost 1.00 pm. It will not be possible for us to continue, even with the cross-examination, today, because we have to vacate -- we have to go to lunch, and after lunch, another Trial Chamber will occupy this courtroom, the only courtroom we have, and, therefore, we will have to adjourn these proceedings until Monday for cross-examination.
